title: Team of Rivals? Toward a New Model of the Corporate Attorney-Client Relationship
pub: Fordham Law Review, Vol. 78, Issue 5, pp. 2067–2136 (2010)
author: David B. Wilkins

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Big Four: Integration matters more than replacement
st.an: The source does not assess Big Four–law firm convergence or multidisciplinary business-service integration. It instead explains changing corporate legal relationships through law-firm consolidation, panel reductions, larger work bundles and deeper dependence on existing clients, offering a materially different account of incumbent adaptation.
qs: As companies shrink the number of outside firms that they use and package even the legal work that they put out for competitive bid in ever-larger bundles, there are fewer opportunities for firms to win new clients.10 5 At the same time, the pressure by even long-standing clients to cut fees has led many firms to try to increase revenues by expanding the volume of work that they do for each client.
This, in turn, has put pressure on firms to find ways to improve the level of service that they give to these increasingly important clients.

st.t: Billable hour: Faster matters need not reduce profits
st.an: The source does not assess whether AI-driven reductions in hours can preserve profits. It reframes the problem around long-term lawyer–client partnerships, associate development and ethical governance, arguing that changing fees alone is insufficient to repair incentives and trust.
qs: By giving both clients and firms a stake in a long-term relationship in which both sides have an interest in the other's success, the new partnerships offer at least some hope of breaking out of this gloomy state of affairs.
78  for example by moving to fixed fees, supporting the broader normative aspects of the relationship discussed in the proceeding section will require ethical as well as contractual support.

st.t: Partnership structure: AI tests governance beyond capital scarcity
st.an: The source does not assess whether AI, capital, ownership or partnership governance constrain law-firm adaptation. Instead, it redirects the governance question toward corporate compliance, advocating shared responsibility across legal and business professionals rather than reliance on a single gatekeeper.
qs: 78  regulatory schemes-that achieving effective compliance is the joint responsibility of legal and business professionals.
To achieve this goal it is necessary to move beyond a regulatory focus that assumes that gatekeeping duties are the sole responsibility of a single actor.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not assess AI’s jagged capabilities, selective deployment or verification. It instead reframes work redesign around durable corporate–outside-firm alliances, emphasising integration, knowledge transfer, reciprocal obligations, alternative pricing and regulation. This is constructively relevant to operating-model and provider-boundary questions, but it advances a materially different, non-AI-centred proposition.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source supports buyer-led reorganisation through insourcing, competitive purchasing and periodic provider review. However, its central model emphasises fewer law-firm relationships, larger bundled assignments and durable integrated alliances rather than task-by-task workflow unbundling; it also does not address AI-driven pricing, junior training or verification.
qs: As with many necessary but expensive services, a growing number decided that it would be cheaper to "make" legal services internally rather than to "buy" them on the open market.

As companies shrink the number of outside firms that they use and package even the legal work that they put out for competitive bid in ever-larger bundles, there are fewer opportunities for firms to win new clients.10 5 At the same time, the pressure by even long-standing clients to cut fees has led many firms to try to increase revenues by expanding the volume of work that they do for each client.

st.t: Big Law economics: Durable value exceeds firm size
st.an: The source accepts that Big Law’s durability depends on economic mechanisms beyond size alone and materially develops the proposition by showing how client cost pressure, panel consolidation and firms’ profit motives can make scale valuable when it deepens major-client relationships. Its Linklaters case also illustrates that selective client concentration, rather than expansion by itself, may improve profitability.
qs: Collectively this wave of consolidation among the world's top law firms has in turn facilitated a new rapprochement between companies and firms.
The net result of all of these trends has been a growing awareness among firms that the best way to ensure their profitability is to leverage their relationships with their existing clients.

st.t: Buyer authority: In-house growth need not displace firms
st.an: The source reinforces the proposition that in-house growth need not displace firms by identifying concrete continuity mechanisms: GC turnover can make incumbent outside lawyers repositories of institutional memory, while switching costs and uncertain gains deter firm replacement. It also cites departmental downsizing as a qualification to aggregate in-house employment growth.
qs: To fill in these gaps, the new GC is likely to look to the accumulated experience and knowledge of the company's primary outside lawyers.

Similarly, general counsels who are contemplating making a move may fear tampering with their existing primary outside counsel relationships for fear that the speculative gains in cost and quality of bringing in a new firm either will not materialize, or will prove not to be worth the time and energy that the GC would have to expend to disrupt the status quo.

st.t: Corporate buyers: Insourcing and partnerships coexist
st.an: The source strongly accepts the shift of purchasing control toward sophisticated in-house counsel while materially developing the cluster’s coexistence thesis through a strategic-alliance model. It argues that corporate departments and outside firms remain interdependent for information and expertise even as they continue competing for work and influence.
qs: More fundamentally, outside firms and in-house lawyers still actively compete with each other for both work and influence.

st.t: Firm tournament: Partnership extends rather than ends competition
st.an: Wilkins accepts that competition persists within durable corporate–law-firm partnerships and materially extends the cluster by connecting client purchasing, firm incentives and junior training. He proposes long-term, non-hourly strategic alliances as a possible way to finance development, while identifying dependency and regulatory risks rather than claiming a proven successor model.
qs: By giving both clients and firms a stake in a long-term relationship in which both sides have an interest in the other's success, the new partnerships offer at least some hope of breaking out of this gloomy state of affairs.

st.t: In-house power: Business integration risks professional capture
st.an: Wilkins accepts the cluster’s core account that stronger, more integrated corporate buyers can improve coordination and accountability while increasing capture risks. He materially develops it through the legal-keiretsu model, proposing reciprocal client–lawyer duties, protection against pressure to breach ethical obligations, shared gatekeeping, and regulatory reinforcement, while treating the model’s effects as provisional.
qs: By instructing outside lawyers to become "partners" with their major clients who are encouraged to see their primary value as helping client teams deploy legal knowledge to maximize competitive advantage, the new strategic alliances between companies and firms risk turning "independent" 92 lawyers into just another consultant serving business ends.

A model of the attorney-client relationship that recognizes that both clients and lawyers have reciprocal obligations of disclosure, forbearance, and fair dealing of the kind characteristic of strategic alliances, I will argue, provides a better foundation for dealing with these increasingly important problems.

st.t: Professional independence: Regulation should follow client vulnerability
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that professional independence depends on institutional conditions rather than bar self-regulation or client control alone. It materially develops that proposition for corporate practice by proposing reciprocal client–lawyer duties, protection for counsel who resist unethical demands, and external regulation that can strengthen gatekeeping, while treating the supporting empirical evidence as preliminary.
qs: A model of the attorney-client relationship that recognizes that both clients and lawyers have reciprocal obligations of disclosure, forbearance, and fair dealing of the kind characteristic of strategic alliances, I will argue, provides a better foundation for dealing with these increasingly important problems.

Given that the bar has often used the ideal of professional independence as a sword to defeat the kinds of external regulation that might actually give corporate lawyers the incentive to resist the improper demands of their powerful clients, we should be particularly careful about uncritically accepting arguments of this kind as a reason not to explore the types of ethical and regulatory alternatives described below.

st.t: Cravath model: Modern firms retain hollowed labels
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s account that intensified client competition weakened traditional firm structures and encouraged lateral hiring, mobility and competition for individual lawyers. Its discussion of discarded lateral-hiring taboos and recruits expected to bring clients directly aligns with the shift away from internal promotion and durable institutional relationships.
qs: 58 Suffice it to say that as competition for clients intensified, many firms began to compete aggressively for lawyers as well.

Traditional taboos against lateral hiring of associates-and eventually partners-were discarded as firms moved to poach talented lawyers from their competitors, lawyers who were expected to bring their clients with them in tow.

st.t: General counsel: Strategic authority carries guardian tension
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s account of general counsel gaining strategic authority over outside providers while assuming a dual business-partner and guardian role. It also reinforces the synthesis’s qualifications: greater in-house capacity did not reliably contain external spending or guarantee effective oversight, and continuing dependence on outside counsel complicates any simple displacement narrative.
qs: General counsel were therefore the lawyers who should be entrusted with the role of being both a "partner" to the business in achieving its objectives and the "guardian" of the company's 63 long-term reputation and values.

Notwithstanding a significant investment in building up in-house capacities, many companies discovered that their outside spending on law firms continued to escalate throughout the 1990s and into the first decade of the twenty-first century.

kp.k: Strategic alliances challenge the traditional agency model
kp.d: Wilkins advances a historical and theoretical argument about corporate legal services, rather than a claim about AI. He argues descriptively and normatively that relationships between large corporations and their principal outside firms increasingly resemble strategic alliances or a legal keiretsu. Reciprocal obligations of disclosure, forbearance and fair dealing offer a better foundation than a model concentrating rights in clients and duties in lawyers.
qs: the agency model is no longer a helpful template for understanding the relationship between corporations and their outside firms.
My claim is both descriptive and normative.
Clients have only rights, not obligations.

kp.k: Historical lawyer independence depended partly on market power
kp.d: The article describes the traditional corporate relationship as a durable bilateral monopoly supported by information asymmetry, switching costs and belief in law's autonomy. These conditions enabled institutional knowledge, training and public-regarding advice, but also insulated firms from accountability over costs and service. Wilkins cautions that the historical periods are stylized and that lawyers did not necessarily fulfill their professed gatekeeping ideals.
qs: these early lawyers aspired to be wise counselors
Clients were literally passed down from senior partners to their most promising protg6-who had already worked on the client's matters for several years before assuming their new role.
companies began to feel that firms were using their market power to pad the partners' pockets at their expense.

kp.k: In-house expertise shifted purchasing power toward clients
kp.d: During the 1980s and 1990s, sophisticated legal departments internalized diagnostic and referral functions, brought work inside and subjected outside firms to competitive purchasing and detailed oversight. GE under Ben Heineman serves as a stylized example: by the conclusion of his tenure in 2006 its legal department had over 1000 lawyers. Wilkins acknowledges that GE retained productive partnerships on important matters, but characterizes the dominant ethos as selecting individual lawyers for particular assignments.
qs: corporations began internalizing these functions by building sophisticated and extensive in-house legal staffs.
Law firms were made to compete for work in "beauty contests" or "bake offs"
general counsel sought to bifurcate the two parts of the lawyer's role as well.

kp.k: Spot contracting did not reliably deliver expected benefits
kp.d: Wilkins reports that growing in-house capabilities and tighter monitoring did not necessarily contain outside spending or improve satisfaction. In-house lawyers claimed the trusted-adviser and gatekeeping roles while outside counsel became more episodic specialists, but continuing costs, dissatisfaction and post-Enron regulatory demands encouraged reconsideration of this division of responsibility.
qs: many companies discovered that their outside spending on law firms continued to escalate throughout the 1990s and into the first decade of the twenty-first century.
Nor were all of the resources being devoted to monitoring and controlling law firms resulting in increased levels of client satisfaction.

kp.k: Convergence concentrated important work among fewer firms
kp.d: DuPont reduced its significant U.S. firm relationships from 350 to 35 in two years, and later reduced international patent and trademark firms from 300 to 48, with 28 handling more than 95% of that work. The Harvard purchasing study comprised 43 GC interviews and 139 survey responses, a 28% response rate, with 166 unique companies overall. As of 2003, 80% of sampled companies assigned 80% of important work to twenty-five or fewer firms; almost 40% used ten or fewer. The trend was uneven: between 2003 and 2006, 40% reduced firms accounting for 80% of total spending, just under 30% increased them, and the remaining 30% were essentially unchanged.
qs: In just two years, DuPont reduced the number of U.S. law firms to whom it gave significant business from 350 to 35.

In less than a year, the company reduced the number of firms handling its international work in this area from 300 to 48, with 28 of these handling more than 95% of the company's international patent and trademark work.

kp.k: Clients valued business understanding and predictable expenditure
kp.d: Convergence sought bargaining power, bundled pricing and budget predictability, but was not confined to commodity work. Wilkins reports that premium assignments could reward preferred providers for discounts elsewhere. A BTI survey illustrates differing definitions of client focus: 21% of GCs identified understanding the business, compared with 10% of firm respondents; 21% of firm respondents instead identified doing what was best for the client, compared with 3% of GCs. These are reported customer preferences, not demonstrated effects of convergence.
qs: General counsel, like every other corporate manager, have to ensure that their department's spending stays within budgetary limits.
companies promise firms that they will also have preferential access to the company's more lucrative business.
But companies mean something different by "quality service" than most commentators-and most outside lawyers-typically 85 think.

kp.k: Consolidation encouraged firms to deepen major client relationships
kp.d: Wilkins connects firm growth, international expansion and mergers with efforts to concentrate on major clients, cross-sell services and increase work per relationship. His Linklaters example, drawing on Ashish Nanda's case study, describes pruning smaller clients and asking lawyers or offices unable to support priority global clients to leave. The reported result was higher profitability, but the article does not treat every firm's growth as simply a response to client demand.
qs: The result is that large global companies increasingly interact with law firms that are themselves large and globalized.
The firm therefore instituted a rigorous-and in the eyes of many, draconian-policy to "prune" its client list.
The result was a dramatic increase in the firm's profitability.

kp.k: Integrated teams made organizational boundaries more permeable
kp.d: Preferred-provider systems increasingly involved shared practices and technology, cross-firm teams, client-specific teams, reciprocal training, secondments and sometimes joint recruiting. Drawing on Robert Rosen, Wilkins connects these practices with corporate downsizing, outsourcing and self-managing project teams. These arrangements change coordination between buyers and providers without eliminating competition for work, influence or personnel.
qs: As companies and firms have moved closer together, the boundaries that have traditionally separated lawyer and client have grown increasingly permeable.
many firms have adopted dedicated "client teams" to service their most important client relationships.
More fundamentally, outside firms and in-house lawyers still actively compete with each other for both work and influence.

kp.k: GC mobility could increase reliance on outside institutional memory
kp.d: Unpublished research by John Coates reported that in 2005 GC turnover was 29%, compared with CEO turnover of 15%. Wilkins hypothesizes that new GCs may rely on established outside counsel to learn company history, while departing GCs may avoid disruptive provider changes. Downsizing and variation in department size could reinforce this mechanism; these consequences are proposed interpretations, not established causal findings.
qs: Thus in 2005, nearly twice as many GCs turned over as CEOs (29% to 15%).
High turnover rates among GCs are likely to increase the degree to which companies rely on their primary outside law firms.
To fill in these gaps, the new GC is likely to look to the accumulated experience and knowledge of the company's primary outside lawyers.

kp.k: Supplier alliances illustrate cooperation alongside continuing competition
kp.d: The Chrysler analogy supplies an organizational mechanism rather than legal-market causal evidence. Moving away from lowest-bidder purchasing, Chrysler adopted cross-functional teams, fewer suppliers, longer commitments and shared savings. Its SCORE program reportedly grew from 875 suggestions worth $170.8 million in its first year to 5300 suggestions generating $1.7 billion in savings when assessed in 1995. Wilkins uses this example to explain how mutual dependence and voice can generate joint gains, while later supplier distress illustrates concentrated relationship risk.
qs: Suppliers were given long-term contracts for the life of the vehicle and beyond.
Chrysler agreed to share half of any resulting cost savings with the company that made the suggestion.
Keiretsus link the fate of those in the strategic alliance in good times and in bad

kp.k: Tyco experimented with risk sharing and prevention incentives
kp.d: Tyco consolidated work from 250 firms into Eversheds, initially confronting serious implementation difficulties. The revised arrangement included 10,000 hours of commodity work at reduced rates, unpaid initial overruns, shared savings from underruns and outcome adjustments for litigation under $1 million: a twenty-five percent success premium or ten percent loss penalty. Additional bonuses rewarded client satisfaction, diversity and a fifteen percent reduction in lawsuits. Premium work remained outside the guarantee. Wilkins presents these as contractual attempts to align incentives, not proof that every feature succeeded.
qs: For basic "commodity work," the company agrees to pay Eversheds for 10,000 hours of work at reduced rates.
The firm will take home another six-figure bonus if it is able to reduce the number of lawsuits filed against Tyco by fifteen percent over the number filed in the previous year.
To give Eversheds the chance to meet this target, Tyco promises to give the firm access (at the law firm's expense) to Tyco's business processes and people.

kp.k: Tyco's renewal modified rather than preserved original incentives
kp.d: In fall 2009, Tyco and Eversheds renewed for another two years, removing many bonus provisions in favor of fixed and discounted fees while expanding major projects and intellectual-property work. The article reports that Eversheds met customer-satisfaction targets and exceeded litigation-reduction targets but missed its diversity target. Wilkins treats continuation as evidence of relationship durability while acknowledging uncertainty about why particular incentives were dropped.
qs: In the fall of 2009, the two parties agreed to renew their exclusive deal for another two years.
In the previous two years, Eversheds met the contract's goal for improving customer satisfaction and exceeded the target for reducing litigation filed against Tyco.
the fact that the diversity targets were also omitted even though Eversheds failed to meet this goal suggest that it may not be a complete explanation.

kp.k: Embedded relationships create switching costs and concentrated vulnerability
kp.d: The purchasing survey found that nearly 80% of GCs had terminated an important firm relationship at most once or twice between 2003 and 2006; 31% had never done so, 21% had done so more than twice and 1% frequently. Wilkins warns that low termination does not imply satisfaction. Shared knowledge and infrastructure make exit harder, exposing companies to firm failure and firms to client collapse, acquisitions or restrictions on other relationships. Howrey's loss of its Unocal arrangement after Chevron's acquisition illustrates this risk.
qs: The fact that companies rarely terminate important law firm relationships should not be taken to mean that companies are generally satisfied with the service that they are receiving.
As the smaller and more junior member of the partnership, firms face substantially more risks from the failure of their primary clients than the other way around.
Howrey ultimately lost its preferred provider deal when Unocal was acquired by Chevron, which already had its own law firm relationships.

kp.k: Alternative fees may restore incentives for junior training
kp.d: Wilkins argues that client resistance to paying for first- and second-year associates, combined with partners' reluctance to absorb training costs, produced inadequate development. Long-term relationships and pricing detached from each junior hour could make observation and supervised participation jointly valuable. He reports supporting associations between dissatisfaction with training and intentions to leave, but does not establish that alternative fees causally improve training or retention.
qs: Clients, weary of an ever-changing cast of untrained-and undoubtedly relatively unproductive-junior lawyers shuffling in and out of their projects, are increasingly unwilling to pay for the work of first-year and second-year associates.
At the same time, partners eager to boost their profits per partner are unwilling to absorb this cost either.
Once they are freed from the tyranny of hourly billings, clients not only don't mind a young associate sitting in on a deposition or listening in on a phone call, they applaud the process.

kp.k: Closer relationships have ambiguous implications for professional independence
kp.d: Wilkins acknowledges that major-client dependence and identification with business goals may weaken gatekeeping. Conversely, sustained relationships can give outside lawyers information, access and incentives to prevent misconduct that fragmented assignments deny them. He argues that client and firm interests in long-term legitimacy can support professional values, but warns that market incentives may favor appearances rather than substantive independence or diversity. He explicitly characterizes his implications analysis as preliminary and speculative.
qs: My observations in this section will therefore be both preliminary and speculative.
strategic alliances don't so much eliminate the space for gatekeeping as reorient its dynamics.
The bottom line is that too much focus on the bottom line runs the risk of promoting the appearance of a commitment to diversity at the expense of producing real results.

kp.k: Reciprocal ethics require legal and institutional enforcement
kp.d: Wilkins recommends moving beyond unilateral client control toward mutual trust, disclosure and limits on opportunistic pressure, including some penalty for dismissing counsel for refusing to breach ethical duties. He interprets the ABA's 2002–2003 changes to Model Rules 1.6 and 1.13 as partial protections against client manipulation, not a complete reciprocal regime. Because professional rules cannot bind nonlawyer clients, substantive law and enforcement must supplement ethical norms. His discussion concerns Model Rules and their relationship to regulation, not uniform state adoption.
qs: At a minimum, the logic of these new relationships suggests that clients should pay some penalty for dismissing an attorney for failing to breach one of the lawyer's own ethical duties.
A complete account of the ethics of lawyer-client strategic alliances would have to define client obligations as well as lawyer rights.
Whatever their other virtues, the Model Rules of Professional Conduct cannot bind nonlawyers.

kp.k: Compliance should remain a shared organizational responsibility
kp.d: Wilkins argues that regulatory enforcement and internal compliance systems can reinforce independence. He reports Tanina Rostain's interviews with ten GCs as limited, preliminary evidence that Sarbanes-Oxley strengthened their authority over legal risk. He distinguishes his position from John Coffee's proposed independent disclosure counsel: concentrating gatekeeping in one specialist could encourage other lawyers to abandon it and companies to treat that specialist as a government agent. Effective compliance instead requires coordination among inside and outside lawyers, managers and other professionals.
qs: Although the evidence is both preliminary and mixed, there is at least some indication that these regulatory changes are having a positive effect on lawyer independence.
it is entirely possible that Coffee's proposal could drive the vast majority of lawyers not acting as disclosure counsel to give up their gatekeeping roles altogether
achieving effective compliance is the joint responsibility of legal and business professionals.

kp.k: Crisis predictions remain conditional on changing market structures
kp.d: Writing during the financial crisis, Wilkins predicts that cost pressure, legal-department cuts and stronger regulation could accelerate partnering while also threatening training, diversity and pro bono commitments. He identifies the ACC Value Challenge as a contemporaneous attempt to institutionalize mutual duties, business understanding and training. He expressly disclaims certainty about the market's direction and notes that increasing mobility and client emphasis on teams rather than firms might undermine organization-level alliances.
qs: Needless to say, I do not pretend to know where all of this is heading even in the next six to twelve months, let alone in the next five to ten years.
As in-house legal offices shrink, companies are likely to become even more dependent upon their relationships with outside firms.
the important unit of analysis might shift significantly-undermining the ability of "companies" and "firms" to forge the kind of cooperative relationships examined here.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: No qualifying AI-related claim or prediction is present.
pts.d: Wilkins's article concerns changes in corporate attorney-client relationships, not artificial intelligence. Its central claim is that relationships between large corporate clients and outside law firms increasingly resemble strategic alliances rather than traditional principal-agent relationships. It attributes this development to convergence of outside counsel panels, law firm consolidation, organizational integration, corporate restructuring, and in-house counsel mobility. These are not presented as AI-driven changes. References to standardization, technology platforms, and online legal-service intermediaries do not establish an AI claim.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The article supplies evidence about corporate legal purchasing and partnering, but none about AI's effects.
pts.d: Wilkins draws on interviews and survey research concerning S&P 500 legal departments, examples such as DuPont's convergence program and the Tyco/Eversheds relationship, and research on supplier alliances. These support the article's organizational and legal-market arguments, not findings about AI adoption, performance, substitution, or augmentation.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.d: Published in 2010, the article examines historical developments in corporate legal services and the possible consequences of the contemporary financial crisis. Wilkins explicitly qualifies his assessment of emerging strategic alliances as preliminary and speculative. Those qualifications should not be repurposed as forecasts about AI.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected constituencies are identified for organizational change, not AI-related change.
pts.d: The article addresses large companies, in-house legal departments, large outside law firms, their lawyers, and the public affected by corporate lawyers' gatekeeping. It does not identify any constituency as experiencing AI-driven changes in work, employment, pricing, or service access.
